answer:
Based on my comprehensive research of the Israeli electoral system and the official sources, I need to clarify an important point before answering your question.

**In Israel, Supreme Court justices are not directly elected by the public.** They are appointed through a different process than general elections. Here's what actually happens:

## How Supreme Court Justices Are Selected in Israel

According to the information from `elections.il.gov` and other official sources:

1. **Judicial Selection Committee (JSC)** - This committee selects Supreme Court justice candidates. It consists of:
   - Three Supreme Court justices
   - Two representatives from the Israel Bar Association  
   - Four politicians (three from the coalition government, one from the opposition)

2. **Appointment Process**: For Supreme Court justices specifically, **7 out of 9 committee members must agree** to the appointment. This requires broad consensus across both professional and political members.

3. **President's Role**: Once the JSC agrees on a candidate, the President formally appoints them.

## Your Question's Premise Issue

Because Supreme Court justices are **appointed rather than directly elected**, there are:
- No public general primaries or general elections for Supreme Court seats
- No public vote counts between candidates
- No "1st vs 2nd place finisher" margin calculations from public ballots

## What Might Be Confused

It appears there may be some confusion in the terminology. If you're interested in:

- **Knesset Legislative Elections** (2020, 2022, etc.) - These ARE direct public elections where vote margins can be calculated
- **Proposed Reforms** - There have been debates about allowing popular elections for some judicial positions, but these have not been implemented
- **A Different Country** - Some countries do hold direct elections for supreme court positions

**If you meant Knesset legislative elections instead of Supreme Court Justice selections**, please clarify and I'd be happy to provide that information about those elections' vote margins!

Title: Elections in Israel
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,9,10,11,12
**Elections in Israel** are based on nationwide proportional representation. The electoral threshold is currently set at 3.25%,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-1) with the number of seats a party receives in the Knesset being proportional to the number of votes it receives.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-3) The Knesset is elected for a four-year term, although most governments have not served a full term and snap elections are a frequent occurrence. Israel has a multi-party system based on coalition governments as no party has ever won a majority of seats in a national election, although the Alignment briefly held a majority following its formation by an alliance of several different parties prior to the 1969 elections. Suffrage is universal for all Israeli citizens above the age of 18. Israeli citizens living abroad have to travel to Israel in order to vote, but Israeli citizens living within the Israeli-occupied territories may vote from within those territories.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-6) Voting booths are made available on Israeli ships. Elections are overseen by the Central Elections Committee, and are held according to the Knesset Elections Law. Israel was ranked 53rd most electoral democratic country in the world according to V-Dem Democracy indices in 2026, having been downgraded from "liberal democracy" to "electoral democracy" in 2024.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-vdem_dataset-7)Municipal elections normally take place every five years, though the 2024 elections – originally scheduled for October 2023 – were postponed due to the onset of the Gaza war.

## Electoral procedure
[edit]
Ballot envelope, 2019
Under normal circumstances, Israel's Basic Law requires national elections for the Knesset to take place on a Tuesday in the Jewish month of Cheshvan (early October through mid-November) four years following the previous elections. However, it is possible, and it often happens, that early elections can take place prior to the date set in the basic law.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-mfa-8) Early elections can be called by a vote of the majority of Knesset members and normally occur on occasions of political stalemate and of the inability of the government to get the parliament's support for its policies. Failure to get the annual budget bill approved by the Knesset by 31 March (3 months after the start of the fiscal year) also leads automatically to early elections. It is also possible to postpone the date of the election by a special majority of the Knesset members.
Israel uses the closed-list method of party-list proportional representation;[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-IPS-9) thus citizens vote for their preferred party and not for any individual candidates. The 120 seats in the Knesset are then assigned proportionally to each party, provided that the party vote count met the 3.25% electoral threshold. The [D'Hondt method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D'Hondt_method "D'Hondt method") is used for marginal votes, slightly favouring the bigger parties.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-IPS-9) Parties may form electoral alliances and run as a single unified party so as to gain enough collective votes to meet the threshold (if so, the alliance _as a whole_ must meet the threshold, not the individual parties) and thus be allocated seats. The relatively low threshold makes representation of minor parties more likely under the Israeli electoral system than many comparable systems used in other countries. Two parties can make an agreement so that both parties' sum of surplus votes are combined, and if the combined surplus votes amount to an extra seat, the extra seat goes to the party with the greater number of surplus votes.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-10)

## Electoral procedure
Voting begins 12 days before election day for the general public in Israeli diplomatic missions worldwide for Israelis serving abroad in an official capacity and their families, and for Israeli sailors on Israeli ships at sea. Polling stations for serving soldiers open 72 hours before election day and soldiers may cast their votes from then up to the end of the election.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-11) Election day is a legally mandated national holiday. Most public polling stations are open between 7:00 AM and 10:00 PM, though if voters are still in line at 10:00 PM, the station will remain open until everyone has voted. Polling stations in small communities with fewer than 350 residents, hospitals, and prisons are open between 8:00 AM and 8:00 PM.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-12) Patients and staff in hospitals not able to vote during election hours are entitled to special permits allowing them to vote after polling stations in hospitals are closed to everyone else.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-13)

## Electoral procedure
Every resident eligible to vote is assigned to a particular polling station close to their registered address, which maintains a list of all voters eligible to vote at that station. At the polling station, officials check the identification of voters to ensure that they are assigned to that particular station, check off their names in the list of voters for that station, and hand the voter an envelope. The voter selects the ballot slip of their party of choice behind a divider, places the slip into the envelope, then emerges from behind the partition to place it in the ballot box.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-:0-14) Special polling stations are set up in hospitals, prisons, diplomatic missions abroad, military bases, [women's shelters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_shelter "Women's shelter"), and Israeli ships to enable medical professionals, patients, diplomats and their families, Jewish Agency staff abroad, soldiers, prison inmates and staff, sailors, and residents of women's shelters to vote. Polling stations with accessibility for the handicapped are set up around the country and police officers on duty may vote at any polling station. However, to ensure that nobody votes twice, as they are still assigned to a particular polling station close to their registered place of residence, they must vote with what are referred to as double envelopes. The envelope containing their ballot slip is placed into a larger envelope which also contains their identifying information so that it can be checked against the list of voters at their assigned polling station to see if they were marked as having voted there before their double envelope vote is counted. Aside from double envelope voters, all citizens may vote only at their registered polling place.

## Electoral procedure
Once a regular polling station closes, officials at the polling station count the votes and send a document recording the results and the ballot box with the ballot slips inside it to one of 25 vote counting centers nationwide, where the documents are checked for any irregularities, then entered into the Central Elections Committee's software system, a closed system not connected to the Internet, and rechecked. Any irregularities detected by the software are brought to the attention of a district court judge present at the station throughout the vote counting process, who adjudicates all such cases. The results are published by the Central Elections Committee.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-:0-14) The double envelope votes are brought to the Knesset and counted after all other votes have been counted. One team checks the identification details in the outer envelope against the list of voters at the person's assigned polling station to see if their name has been crossed out, which would mean that they had voted twice. The envelopes containing the ballot slips are then passed on to another team that opens them and counts the votes, thus preserving the anonymity of the votes.
Any Israeli citizen over 21 may be elected to the Knesset, except holders of several high positions in the civil service and officers or career soldiers (those should resign from their post before the elections), soldiers in compulsory service, and felons who were convicted and sentenced to prison terms exceeding three months (until seven years after their prison term expired).
The following people may not serve as a Member of Knesset (MK) due to their conflicting functions:[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-15)
1.   The President of the State of Israel  
2.   The two Chief Rabbis of the State of Israel  
3.   Any judge in the judicial system, so long as they still hold office  
4.   Any _dayan_, or judge in the Rabbinical Court system, so long as they still hold office  
5.   The State Comptroller  
6.   Rabbis or Ministers of religions, while receiving salaries for such a position  
7.   Senior state employees and senior army officers of such grades or ranks and in such functions as shall be determined by law

## Electoral procedure
The following prevents a party from running a list in Knesset elections:[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-16)
1.   Negating the State of Israel as the state of the Jewish people  
2.   Negating the democratic nature of the State  
3.   Incitement to racism  
4.   Support of armed struggle against the State of Israel
After an election, the President, following consultations with the elected party leaders, chooses the Knesset member most likely to have the ability to form a viable (coalition) government. While this typically is the leader of the party receiving the most seats, it is not required to be so. In the event a party wins 61 or more seats in an election, it can form a viable government without having to form a coalition. However, no party has ever won more than 56 seats in an election; thus, a coalition has always been required.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-mfa-8) That member has up to 42 days to negotiate with the different parties, and then present his or her government to the Knesset for a vote of confidence. If the Knesset approves the proposed government (by a vote of at least 61 members), he or she becomes Prime Minister.

## Electoral procedure
As the coalitions often prove highly unstable - given the number and diverse views of the political parties involved - parties (or portions thereof) quite commonly leave them. However, so long as the coalition has at least 61 members (and it is free to recruit from parties not originally in the coalition) it is entitled to remain in power. Such a case occurred with the 19th Knesset: Ehud Barak and four other members left the Labor Party in 2011 to form the Independence Party, and continued their alignment with Likud, while the remaining eight Labor members remained with the party, but left the coalition; after all the changes, the Likud coalition retained the support of the minimum 61 members, and so, it remained in power. If a coalition fails a motion of no confidence, it ceases to be in power, unless the motion names a specific replacement to be the prime minister. That individual then has a prescribed amount of time to form a new coalition, and new elections are called if this attempt is not successful (known as a constructive vote of no confidence).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-17)
Israel has three sources of funding political campaigns: state funding (which makes up the majority), public donations and registration fees and other sources.
A single funding unit, which is calculated using a formula, is equivalent to 1.83 million NIS, as of September 2026.
Parties which hold Knesset seats are allocated higher amounts than a new party that has won a Knesset seat. If a party at a minimum reaches one per cent of the vote, but does not reach the electoral threshold, it is given one funding unit.
On the other hand, if a party competes in an election, but wins less than one per cent of the vote, it is allocated no funding units.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-18)

Israel’s October 27 election ended in deadlock, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival Gadi Eisenkot with a clear path to a majority.
With nearly all votes counted, Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious coalition secured 53 seats, and former military chief Eisenkot’s bloc of right-wing and centre-left factions secured 48. Israel’s two Arab-dominated parties secured a record 19 seats. Netanyahu’s bloc rules out forming a coalition with the Arab parties. Eisenkot has also shunned them, citing a lack of shared values with parties representing the country’s 21% Palestinian minority.
With the votes now tallied, Israel’s President Isaac Herzog will hold consulations with party representatives before tapping the candidate whom he deems has the best chance to form a government. That is expected after November 4.

Benjamin Netanyahu
Likud
Likud has been in power almost consecutively since 1977, when it toppled the Labour party that had dominated Israeli politics since independence in 1948. Likud's hegemony before Netanyahu was marked by the expansion of Jewish settlements on land that Palestinians seek for a state, a landmark peace treatise with Egypt and the 1982 invasion of Lebanon. Netanyahu, who led Likud in the 1990s and then again from 2005, forged diplomatic ties with more Arab countries in the 2020 Abraham accords and held failed peace talks with the Palestinians. His present term in office has seen Likud embrace right-wing populism with a bid to curb the powers of Israel's Supreme Court. Likud has kept up its alliance with far-right parties who have backed Netanyahu’s conduct of wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran and driven settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. Likud’s popularity plummeted soon after the October 7 Hamas attack.
Itamar Ben-Gvir

# Israel election results
### Netanyahu-led bloc
Jewish Power (Otzma Yehudit)
Led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who was convicted in 2007 of racist incitement against Arabs and backing a group considered by Israel and the United States to be a terrorist organization. Under his leadership, Jewish Power authored legislation promoting capital punishment for convicted Palestinian militants. As minister, Ben-Gvir toughened prison conditions for Palestinians jailed in Israel and eased regulations on gun ownership for Israelis. He has also advocated for the expulsion of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip.
Bezalel Smotrich
Religious Zionism
Led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, Religious Zionism represents Israel’s small but powerful ideological settler movement. The party advocates for the annexation of the West Bank, which they view as the biblical bedrock of the Jewish people, and resettlement of Gaza. Holding a second portfolio in Israel’s defence ministry, Smotrich has spearheaded Israel's rapid expansion of West Bank settlements, voicing his hope that it would ‘bury’ the idea of a Palestinian state.
Ofer Winter
People of Israel
A new party founded by Ofer Winter, a right-wing former brigadier general who has been critical of Netanyahu but has also said he wants to be part of a right-wing coalition led by the incumbent. People of Israel wants tougher action against Hamas and incentives for Palestinians to leave Gaza. At the same time, it is aligned with main opposition parties demanding more ultra-Orthodox Jews serve in the military. Winter's party has been teetering on the vote threshold, falling below it in some polls and just passing it in others.
Aryeh Deri

## Electoral procedure
[edit]
Ballot envelope, 2019
Under normal circumstances, Israel's Basic Law requires national elections for the Knesset to take place on a Tuesday in the Jewish month of Cheshvan (early October through mid-November) four years following the previous elections. However, it is possible, and it often happens, that early elections can take place prior to the date set in the basic law.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-mfa-8) Early elections can be called by a vote of the majority of Knesset members and normally occur on occasions of political stalemate and of the inability of the government to get the parliament's support for its policies. Failure to get the annual budget bill approved by the Knesset by 31 March (3 months after the start of the fiscal year) also leads automatically to early elections. It is also possible to postpone the date of the election by a special majority of the Knesset members.
Israel uses the closed-list method of party-list proportional representation;[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-IPS-9) thus citizens vote for their preferred party and not for any individual candidates. The 120 seats in the Knesset are then assigned proportionally to each party, provided that the party vote count met the 3.25% electoral threshold. The [D'Hondt method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D'Hondt_method "D'Hondt method") is used for marginal votes, slightly favouring the bigger parties.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-IPS-9) Parties may form electoral alliances and run as a single unified party so as to gain enough collective votes to meet the threshold (if so, the alliance _as a whole_ must meet the threshold, not the individual parties) and thus be allocated seats. The relatively low threshold makes representation of minor parties more likely under the Israeli electoral system than many comparable systems used in other countries. Two parties can make an agreement so that both parties' sum of surplus votes are combined, and if the combined surplus votes amount to an extra seat, the extra seat goes to the party with the greater number of surplus votes.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-10)
texts.2:
## Electoral procedure
Voting begins 12 days before election day for the general public in Israeli diplomatic missions worldwide for Israelis serving abroad in an official capacity and their families, and for Israeli sailors on Israeli ships at sea. Polling stations for serving soldiers open 72 hours before election day and soldiers may cast their votes from then up to the end of the election.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-11) Election day is a legally mandated national holiday. Most public polling stations are open between 7:00 AM and 10:00 PM, though if voters are still in line at 10:00 PM, the station will remain open until everyone has voted. Polling stations in small communities with fewer than 350 residents, hospitals, and prisons are open between 8:00 AM and 8:00 PM.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-12) Patients and staff in hospitals not able to vote during election hours are entitled to special permits allowing them to vote after polling stations in hospitals are closed to everyone else.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-13)
texts.3:
## Electoral procedure
Every resident eligible to vote is assigned to a particular polling station close to their registered address, which maintains a list of all voters eligible to vote at that station. At the polling station, officials check the identification of voters to ensure that they are assigned to that particular station, check off their names in the list of voters for that station, and hand the voter an envelope. The voter selects the ballot slip of their party of choice behind a divider, places the slip into the envelope, then emerges from behind the partition to place it in the ballot box.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-:0-14) Special polling stations are set up in hospitals, prisons, diplomatic missions abroad, military bases, [women's shelters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_shelter "Women's shelter"), and Israeli ships to enable medical professionals, patients, diplomats and their families, Jewish Agency staff abroad, soldiers, prison inmates and staff, sailors, and residents of women's shelters to vote. Polling stations with accessibility for the handicapped are set up around the country and police officers on duty may vote at any polling station. However, to ensure that nobody votes twice, as they are still assigned to a particular polling station close to their registered place of residence, they must vote with what are referred to as double envelopes. The envelope containing their ballot slip is placed into a larger envelope which also contains their identifying information so that it can be checked against the list of voters at their assigned polling station to see if they were marked as having voted there before their double envelope vote is counted. Aside from double envelope voters, all citizens may vote only at their registered polling place.
texts.4:
## Electoral procedure
Once a regular polling station closes, officials at the polling station count the votes and send a document recording the results and the ballot box with the ballot slips inside it to one of 25 vote counting centers nationwide, where the documents are checked for any irregularities, then entered into the Central Elections Committee's software system, a closed system not connected to the Internet, and rechecked. Any irregularities detected by the software are brought to the attention of a district court judge present at the station throughout the vote counting process, who adjudicates all such cases. The results are published by the Central Elections Committee.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-:0-14) The double envelope votes are brought to the Knesset and counted after all other votes have been counted. One team checks the identification details in the outer envelope against the list of voters at the person's assigned polling station to see if their name has been crossed out, which would mean that they had voted twice. The envelopes containing the ballot slips are then passed on to another team that opens them and counts the votes, thus preserving the anonymity of the votes.
Any Israeli citizen over 21 may be elected to the Knesset, except holders of several high positions in the civil service and officers or career soldiers (those should resign from their post before the elections), soldiers in compulsory service, and felons who were convicted and sentenced to prison terms exceeding three months (until seven years after their prison term expired).
The following people may not serve as a Member of Knesset (MK) due to their conflicting functions:[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-15)
1.   The President of the State of Israel  
2.   The two Chief Rabbis of the State of Israel  
3.   Any judge in the judicial system, so long as they still hold office  
4.   Any _dayan_, or judge in the Rabbinical Court system, so long as they still hold office  
5.   The State Comptroller  
6.   Rabbis or Ministers of religions, while receiving salaries for such a position  
7.   Senior state employees and senior army officers of such grades or ranks and in such functions as shall be determined by law
texts.5:
## Electoral procedure
The following prevents a party from running a list in Knesset elections:[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-16)
1.   Negating the State of Israel as the state of the Jewish people  
2.   Negating the democratic nature of the State  
3.   Incitement to racism  
4.   Support of armed struggle against the State of Israel
After an election, the President, following consultations with the elected party leaders, chooses the Knesset member most likely to have the ability to form a viable (coalition) government. While this typically is the leader of the party receiving the most seats, it is not required to be so. In the event a party wins 61 or more seats in an election, it can form a viable government without having to form a coalition. However, no party has ever won more than 56 seats in an election; thus, a coalition has always been required.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-mfa-8) That member has up to 42 days to negotiate with the different parties, and then present his or her government to the Knesset for a vote of confidence. If the Knesset approves the proposed government (by a vote of at least 61 members), he or she becomes Prime Minister.
texts.6:
## Electoral procedure
As the coalitions often prove highly unstable - given the number and diverse views of the political parties involved - parties (or portions thereof) quite commonly leave them. However, so long as the coalition has at least 61 members (and it is free to recruit from parties not originally in the coalition) it is entitled to remain in power. Such a case occurred with the 19th Knesset: Ehud Barak and four other members left the Labor Party in 2011 to form the Independence Party, and continued their alignment with Likud, while the remaining eight Labor members remained with the party, but left the coalition; after all the changes, the Likud coalition retained the support of the minimum 61 members, and so, it remained in power. If a coalition fails a motion of no confidence, it ceases to be in power, unless the motion names a specific replacement to be the prime minister. That individual then has a prescribed amount of time to form a new coalition, and new elections are called if this attempt is not successful (known as a constructive vote of no confidence).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-17)
Israel has three sources of funding political campaigns: state funding (which makes up the majority), public donations and registration fees and other sources.
A single funding unit, which is calculated using a formula, is equivalent to 1.83 million NIS, as of September 2026.
Parties which hold Knesset seats are allocated higher amounts than a new party that has won a Knesset seat. If a party at a minimum reaches one per cent of the vote, but does not reach the electoral threshold, it is given one funding unit.
On the other hand, if a party competes in an election, but wins less than one per cent of the vote, it is allocated no funding units.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-18)

Source: Israel Government
Israel’s October 27 election ended in deadlock, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival Gadi Eisenkot with a clear path to a majority.
With nearly all votes counted, Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious coalition secured 53 seats, and former military chief Eisenkot’s bloc of right-wing and centre-left factions secured 48. Israel’s two Arab-dominated parties secured a record 19 seats. Netanyahu’s bloc rules out forming a coalition with the Arab parties. Eisenkot has also shunned them, citing a lack of shared values with parties representing the country’s 21% Palestinian minority.
With the votes now tallied, Israel’s President Isaac Herzog will hold consulations with party representatives before tapping the candidate whom he deems has the best chance to form a government. That is expected after November 4.

Benjamin Netanyahu
Likud
Likud has been in power almost consecutively since 1977, when it toppled the Labour party that had dominated Israeli politics since independence in 1948. Likud's hegemony before Netanyahu was marked by the expansion of Jewish settlements on land that Palestinians seek for a state, a landmark peace treatise with Egypt and the 1982 invasion of Lebanon. Netanyahu, who led Likud in the 1990s and then again from 2005, forged diplomatic ties with more Arab countries in the 2020 Abraham accords and held failed peace talks with the Palestinians. His present term in office has seen Likud embrace right-wing populism with a bid to curb the powers of Israel's Supreme Court. Likud has kept up its alliance with far-right parties who have backed Netanyahu’s conduct of wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran and driven settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. Likud’s popularity plummeted soon after the October 7 Hamas attack.

# Israel election results
### Netanyahu-led bloc
Jewish Power (Otzma Yehudit)
Led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who was convicted in 2007 of racist incitement against Arabs and backing a group considered by Israel and the United States to be a terrorist organization. Under his leadership, Jewish Power authored legislation promoting capital punishment for convicted Palestinian militants. As minister, Ben-Gvir toughened prison conditions for Palestinians jailed in Israel and eased regulations on gun ownership for Israelis. He has also advocated for the expulsion of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip.
Bezalel Smotrich
Religious Zionism
Led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, Religious Zionism represents Israel’s small but powerful ideological settler movement. The party advocates for the annexation of the West Bank, which they view as the biblical bedrock of the Jewish people, and resettlement of Gaza. Holding a second portfolio in Israel’s defence ministry, Smotrich has spearheaded Israel's rapid expansion of West Bank settlements, voicing his hope that it would ‘bury’ the idea of a Palestinian state.
Ofer Winter
People of Israel
A new party founded by Ofer Winter, a right-wing former brigadier general who has been critical of Netanyahu but has also said he wants to be part of a right-wing coalition led by the incumbent. People of Israel wants tougher action against Hamas and incentives for Palestinians to leave Gaza. At the same time, it is aligned with main opposition parties demanding more ultra-Orthodox Jews serve in the military. Winter's party has been teetering on the vote threshold, falling below it in some polls and just passing it in others.
Aryeh Deri
SHAS, UTJ
Israel's ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties have been Netanyahu's most loyal political allies for almost two decades. But in his present term, they have been angered by his failure to deliver legislation that they have long sought, to exempt religious seminary students from service in Israel’s conscript military, in favour of full-time devotion to religious study**.**

Any irregularities detected by the software are brought to the attention of a district court judge present at the station throughout the vote counting process, who adjudicates all such cases. The results are published by the Central Elections Committee.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-:0-14) The double envelope votes are brought to the Knesset and counted after all other votes have been counted. One team checks the identification details in the outer envelope against the list of voters at the person's assigned polling station to see if their name has been crossed out, which would mean that they had voted twice. The envelopes containing the ballot slips are then passed on to another team that opens them and counts the votes, thus preserving the anonymity of the votes.
Any Israeli citizen over 21 may be elected to the Knesset, except holders of several high positions in the civil service and officers or career soldiers (those should resign from their post before the elections), soldiers in compulsory service, and felons who were convicted and sentenced to prison terms exceeding three months (until seven years after their prison term expired).
The following people may not serve as a Member of Knesset (MK) due to their conflicting functions:[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-15)
1.   The President of the State of Israel  
2.   The two Chief Rabbis of the State of Israel  
3.   Any judge in the judicial system, so long as they still hold office  
4.   Any _dayan_, or judge in the Rabbinical Court system, so long as they still hold office  
5.   The State Comptroller  
6.   Rabbis or Ministers of religions, while receiving salaries for such a position  
7.   Senior state employees and senior army officers of such grades or ranks and in such functions as shall be determined by law

## Electoral procedure
The following prevents a party from running a list in Knesset elections:[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-16)
1.   Negating the State of Israel as the state of the Jewish people  
2.   Negating the democratic nature of the State  
3.   Incitement to racism  
4.   Support of armed struggle against the State of Israel
After an election, the President, following consultations with the elected party leaders, chooses the Knesset member most likely to have the ability to form a viable (coalition) government. While this typically is the leader of the party receiving the most seats, it is not required to be so. In the event a party wins 61 or more seats in an election, it can form a viable government without having to form a coalition. However, no party has ever won more than 56 seats in an election; thus, a coalition has always been required.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-mfa-8) That member has up to 42 days to negotiate with the different parties, and then present his or her government to the Knesset for a vote of confidence. If the Knesset approves the proposed government (by a vote of at least 61 members), he or she becomes Prime Minister.

## Electoral procedure
As the coalitions often prove highly unstable - given the number and diverse views of the political parties involved - parties (or portions thereof) quite commonly leave them. However, so long as the coalition has at least 61 members (and it is free to recruit from parties not originally in the coalition) it is entitled to remain in power. Such a case occurred with the 19th Knesset: Ehud Barak and four other members left the Labor Party in 2011 to form the Independence Party, and continued their alignment with Likud, while the remaining eight Labor members remained with the party, but left the coalition; after all the changes, the Likud coalition retained the support of the minimum 61 members, and so, it remained in power. If a coalition fails a motion of no confidence, it ceases to be in power, unless the motion names a specific replacement to be the prime minister. That individual then has a prescribed amount of time to form a new coalition, and new elections are called if this attempt is not successful (known as a constructive vote of no confidence).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-17)
Israel has three sources of funding political campaigns: state funding (which makes up the majority), public donations and registration fees and other sources.
A single funding unit, which is calculated using a formula, is equivalent to 1.83 million NIS, as of September 2026.
Parties which hold Knesset seats are allocated higher amounts than a new party that has won a Knesset seat. If a party at a minimum reaches one per cent of the vote, but does not reach the electoral threshold, it is given one funding unit.
On the other hand, if a party competes in an election, but wins less than one per cent of the vote, it is allocated no funding units.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Israel#cite_note-18)

Likud
Likud has been in power almost consecutively since 1977, when it toppled the Labour party that had dominated Israeli politics since independence in 1948. Likud's hegemony before Netanyahu was marked by the expansion of Jewish settlements on land that Palestinians seek for a state, a landmark peace treatise with Egypt and the 1982 invasion of Lebanon. Netanyahu, who led Likud in the 1990s and then again from 2005, forged diplomatic ties with more Arab countries in the 2020 Abraham accords and held failed peace talks with the Palestinians. His present term in office has seen Likud embrace right-wing populism with a bid to curb the powers of Israel's Supreme Court. Likud has kept up its alliance with far-right parties who have backed Netanyahu’s conduct of wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran and driven settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. Led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, Religious Zionism represents Israel’s small but powerful ideological settler movement. The party advocates for the annexation of the West Bank, which they view as the biblical bedrock of the Jewish people, and resettlement of Gaza. People of Israel
A new party founded by Ofer Winter, a right-wing former brigadier general who has been critical of Netanyahu but has also said he wants to be part of a right-wing coalition led by the incumbent. People of Israel wants tougher action against Hamas and incentives for Palestinians to leave Gaza. At the same time, it is aligned with main opposition parties demanding more ultra-Orthodox Jews serve in the military. Winter's party has been teetering on the vote threshold, falling below it in some polls and just passing it in others.

opened.information:
Source: https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/netanyahus-party-claims-israeli-election-stolen-as-results-show-him-losing-majority
Title: Netanyahu’s party claims Israeli election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5
JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party on Thursday amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had "stolen" the election, potentially with foreign assistance, as final results showed his bloc had lost its majority in parliament.
The opposition accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population after a historic showing by Arab-led parties in an attempt to delegitimize the election. If the rest of the opposition teams up with Arab parties, a rare and politically risky move, they could potentially form a majority government in parliament, the Knesset.
**WATCH:** Retired Israeli general on what the election results tell us
Results released by election officials on Thursday showed Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member assembly, well below the 68 seats it had controlled at its peak in the previous parliament. His main opposition won 48 seats and Arab-led parties secured the other 19.
The count is complete, but the results still need to be certified and submitted to the country's president next Wednesday.

## Commission to look into possible foreign interference
Netanyahu's party, Likud, has been spreading claims of malfeasance by Arab-led parties since exit polls indicated the prime minister had suffered a setback in Tuesday's vote. But it ramped up the rhetoric after the head of Israel's election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said that "serious suspicions" of foreign interference had been brought before him.
In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims. But given their serious nature, he asked the agency to investigate.
Netanyahu's party responded with an inflammatory statement: "The elections in Israel have been stolen!" it said, claiming — without evidence — that the alleged election interference was "aimed at facilitating a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and toppling of the right wing government."
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu's party were accusing Qatar — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group.
Qatar issued a quick denial, calling the allegations "ridiculous and dangerous."
As it announced its results early Friday, the election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. In a video statement, the commission's acting director general, Dean Livne, did not elaborate, but warned that reports about the probe had been "entirely unfounded."
"It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population," he said.

## Netanyahu's opponents accuse him of undermining vote
Netanyahu's main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, said Likud was trying to delegitimize the results. "They are doing this because they lost," he said.
Eisenkot ridiculed the accusation of foreign interference with a tongue-in-cheek statement, saying: "I welcome the fact that Netanyahu is finally condemning Qatari involvement in the State of Israel."
Netanyahu has long faced accusations that former top aides of his accepted money from Qatar.
By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be positioning himself to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for Eisenkot to join with Arab parties, who could potentially give Eisenkot the backing he needs to oust Netanyahu.
The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to "cast aspersions" on an entire section of the population that "exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner."
The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament. It said that even though an investigation was taking place, "allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless."
The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week.

## Netanyahu campaigned on anti-Arab sentiment
Even ahead of the vote, Netanyahu and Likud painted the Arab-led parties as a danger to Israel, which critics called an attempt to further marginalize Arab citizens. Arab citizens of Palestinian descent make up 20% of the population but are often viewed with suspicion because of their sympathies with other Palestinians.
Those campaign attacks, along with anger over the divisive Netanyahu and his far-right government, brought outraged Arabs to the polls like never before.
On Thursday, Yair Golan, head of the Democrats party, accused Netanyahu of "attempting to undermine the election results through an ugly delegitimization campaign directed against the will of the public — and against the Arab public in particular."
"Netanyahu is working to steal the election," the Arab-led Joint List party asserted Thursday.
The head of the Arab-led Ra'am party, Mansour Abbas, welcomed the investigation into election interference and said his party had nothing to do with the case, while accusing Netanyahu of a campaign of incitement.
President Isaac Herzog called it a "sensitive moment" and called for a full investigation. He warned that "we must not tarnish an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy."

## Difficult decisions are ahead as parties seek coalitions
The developments amplified the difficult decisions for the weeks ahead. Those include whether some Jewish and Arab parties would team up in a historic alliance, or whether some parties that campaigned on ousting Netanyahu would toss that aside and join forces with him.
**WATCH:** What's next for Israel after election produces political gridlock
While the race for a 61-seat majority needed to control the 120-seat Knesset plays out, Netanyahu remains in charge.
If Netanyahu loses office, that would set off a cascade of events that critics say he has desperately sought to avoid. He would be taken to account over yearslong corruption allegations, and an inquiry almost certainly would begin into the security failures that led to the devastating Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

## Eisenkot has left door open to cooperation with Arab-led parties
Even without a role in a coalition, Arab-led parties could assert their growing power by supporting other Netanyahu opponents in the next parliament. That could include electing a new speaker, giving them control of the agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.
Eisenkot has indicated he is open, with conditions, to joining forces with the Arab-led parties. Ahmad Tibi, second on the Arab-led Joint List, told Army Radio the opposition bloc reached out to him to discuss replacing the Knesset speaker, and he told them the party would support the bloc's candidate.
There were small rallies overnight in Tel Aviv, and in far more conservative Jerusalem, in support of a coalition that includes Arab-led parties. Until 2021, no Arab party had joined a coalition government, and that was brief.
If a new government cannot be formed after multiple attempts, Israel would face a new election early next year. On Wednesday, Herzog signaled he wanted to avoid that step – something Eisenkot has said as well.
New elections bring new questions, including whether Arab citizens would again go to the polls in large numbers and whether the tens of thousands of Israelis who flew home to vote would do it again. Many had said they took that step to save the country from Netanyahu.
_Saeed reported from Abu Snan, Israel. Associated Press reporters across Israel contributed._

Title: Netanyahu’s party claims Israeli election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5
JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party on Thursday amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had "stolen" the election, potentially with foreign assistance, as final results showed his bloc had lost its majority in parliament.
The opposition accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population after a historic showing by Arab-led parties in an attempt to delegitimize the election. If the rest of the opposition teams up with Arab parties, a rare and politically risky move, they could potentially form a majority government in parliament, the Knesset.
**WATCH:** Retired Israeli general on what the election results tell us
Results released by election officials on Thursday showed Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member assembly, well below the 68 seats it had controlled at its peak in the previous parliament. His main opposition won 48 seats and Arab-led parties secured the other 19.
The count is complete, but the results still need to be certified and submitted to the country's president next Wednesday.

## Commission to look into possible foreign interference
Netanyahu's party, Likud, has been spreading claims of malfeasance by Arab-led parties since exit polls indicated the prime minister had suffered a setback in Tuesday's vote. But it ramped up the rhetoric after the head of Israel's election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said that "serious suspicions" of foreign interference had been brought before him.
In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims. But given their serious nature, he asked the agency to investigate.
Netanyahu's party responded with an inflammatory statement: "The elections in Israel have been stolen!" it said, claiming — without evidence — that the alleged election interference was "aimed at facilitating a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and toppling of the right wing government."
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu's party were accusing Qatar — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group.
Qatar issued a quick denial, calling the allegations "ridiculous and dangerous."
As it announced its results early Friday, the election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. In a video statement, the commission's acting director general, Dean Livne, did not elaborate, but warned that reports about the probe had been "entirely unfounded."
"It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population," he said.

## Netanyahu's opponents accuse him of undermining vote
Netanyahu's main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, said Likud was trying to delegitimize the results. "They are doing this because they lost," he said.
Eisenkot ridiculed the accusation of foreign interference with a tongue-in-cheek statement, saying: "I welcome the fact that Netanyahu is finally condemning Qatari involvement in the State of Israel."
Netanyahu has long faced accusations that former top aides of his accepted money from Qatar.
By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be positioning himself to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for Eisenkot to join with Arab parties, who could potentially give Eisenkot the backing he needs to oust Netanyahu.
The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to "cast aspersions" on an entire section of the population that "exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner."
The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament. It said that even though an investigation was taking place, "allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless."
The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week.

## Netanyahu campaigned on anti-Arab sentiment
Even ahead of the vote, Netanyahu and Likud painted the Arab-led parties as a danger to Israel, which critics called an attempt to further marginalize Arab citizens. Arab citizens of Palestinian descent make up 20% of the population but are often viewed with suspicion because of their sympathies with other Palestinians.
Those campaign attacks, along with anger over the divisive Netanyahu and his far-right government, brought outraged Arabs to the polls like never before.
On Thursday, Yair Golan, head of the Democrats party, accused Netanyahu of "attempting to undermine the election results through an ugly delegitimization campaign directed against the will of the public — and against the Arab public in particular."
"Netanyahu is working to steal the election," the Arab-led Joint List party asserted Thursday.
The head of the Arab-led Ra'am party, Mansour Abbas, welcomed the investigation into election interference and said his party had nothing to do with the case, while accusing Netanyahu of a campaign of incitement.
President Isaac Herzog called it a "sensitive moment" and called for a full investigation. He warned that "we must not tarnish an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy."

## Difficult decisions are ahead as parties seek coalitions
The developments amplified the difficult decisions for the weeks ahead. Those include whether some Jewish and Arab parties would team up in a historic alliance, or whether some parties that campaigned on ousting Netanyahu would toss that aside and join forces with him.
**WATCH:** What's next for Israel after election produces political gridlock
While the race for a 61-seat majority needed to control the 120-seat Knesset plays out, Netanyahu remains in charge.
If Netanyahu loses office, that would set off a cascade of events that critics say he has desperately sought to avoid. He would be taken to account over yearslong corruption allegations, and an inquiry almost certainly would begin into the security failures that led to the devastating Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

## Eisenkot has left door open to cooperation with Arab-led parties
Even without a role in a coalition, Arab-led parties could assert their growing power by supporting other Netanyahu opponents in the next parliament. That could include electing a new speaker, giving them control of the agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.
Eisenkot has indicated he is open, with conditions, to joining forces with the Arab-led parties. Ahmad Tibi, second on the Arab-led Joint List, told Army Radio the opposition bloc reached out to him to discuss replacing the Knesset speaker, and he told them the party would support the bloc's candidate.
There were small rallies overnight in Tel Aviv, and in far more conservative Jerusalem, in support of a coalition that includes Arab-led parties. Until 2021, no Arab party had joined a coalition government, and that was brief.
If a new government cannot be formed after multiple attempts, Israel would face a new election early next year. On Wednesday, Herzog signaled he wanted to avoid that step – something Eisenkot has said as well.
New elections bring new questions, including whether Arab citizens would again go to the polls in large numbers and whether the tens of thousands of Israelis who flew home to vote would do it again. Many had said they took that step to save the country from Netanyahu.
_Saeed reported from Abu Snan, Israel. Associated Press reporters across Israel contributed._

opened.information:
Source: https://www.atalayar.com/en/gustavo-aristegui/israel-the-final-vote-count-for-the-26th-knesset-and-the-battle-for-government/20261030141354230182.html
Title: Israel: the final vote count for the 26th Knesset and the battle for government
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
1.   Introduction

2.   The complete count confirms the tie: 53-48-19

3.   The actors and geography of a fracture

4.   From the thesis of the "stolen election" to investigation: Shin Bet, Qatar, and the legitimacy of the Arab vote

5.   Government formation: arithmetic, red lines, and scenarios

6.   The external factor: Iran, Hormuz, and Washington's calendar

7.   Regional ripples: Qatar, the Gulf, Morocco, Europe, and Spain

8.   Media Rack

9.   Editorial Commentary

## Introduction
The counting of double-envelope votes concluded on Thursday afternoon, 29 October, settling—pending official proclamation slated for Wednesday, **4 November**—the outcome of Israel's 27 October elections. Figures confirm what tallies have shown since Wednesday evening: the outgoing coalition bloc led by Benjamin Netanyahu secures **53 seats**, the Zionist opposition spearheaded by former Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot gathers **48**, and the two Arab parties total **19**, an all-time record. Neither major camp reaches the **61 seats** required for an absolute majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
The votes of soldiers, police officers, diplomats, prisoners, and hospitalised citizens shifted just a single piece within the governing block: Likud rises to **27 seats** whilst Shas, the Sephardic ultra-orthodox party, drops to **6**, its lowest tally since 1992.
**Israel** has thus delivered a dual and contradictory verdict. It strips Netanyahu of the majority granted in 2022—his bloc sheds eleven seats in four years—yet awards no one a clear mandate to replace them. An alternative exists in numbers, as 67 MPs reject the Prime Minister, but lacks a program, since that negative majority only rounds out with Arab parties that three of the four Zionist opposition leaders pledged not to approach.
With numbers finalised, battle shifted from counting to legitimacy: Likud claims the election was "stolen" by Arab parties, the Central Elections Committee chair asked Shin Bet to probe foreign funding suspicions, and Police find no backing for fraud claims.
All this unfolds as the Gulf ignites once more. Iran's Revolutionary Guard asserts several tankers struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran has yet to reply to US Vice President JD Vance's letter, and **the United States** has asked allies to prepare for a potential resumption of strikes against Iran following the **3 November** midterms.
Forming the next Israeli government, a routine exercise in parliamentary arithmetic during normal times, has turned into a national security equation. This report analyses developments over the past twenty-four hours, their implications, and unfolding scenarios.

## The complete count confirms the tie: 53-48-19
**Facts**
The Central Elections Committee, an independent body chaired by Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, wrapped up counting double-envelope ballots on Thursday afternoon, having kicked off at 01:00 in the Knesset car park in Jerusalem.
According to figures published by _Israel Hayom_, **5,589,836 votes** were tallied across 12,644 polling stations and counting lots—673 corresponding to double envelopes—with 5,564,764 valid and 25,072 invalid. Turnout hit **77.7%**, the highest since 1999, with Arab mobilisation around **80%** compared to roughly 54% in 2022.
Benny Gantz - REUTERS/ NIR ELIAS
The final breakdown stands as follows: Likud, **27 seats**; Yashar!, Eisenkot's party, **21**; B'Yachad, Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid's list, **12**; the Joint List, **11**; Yair Golan's Democrats, **8**; Ra'am, **8**; Avigdor Lieberman's Yisrael Beytenu, **7**; United Judaism of Torah (UTJ), **7**; Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit, **7**; Shas, **6**; and Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism-Zehut, **6**. Likud secures **20.5%** of valid votes and Yashar!, **16.1%**. Yoaz Hendel's Reservists (**2.72%**) and retired general Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael (**1.68%**) fall beneath the 3.25% threshold, equating to roughly 180,900 votes under the full count.

## The complete count confirms the tie: 53-48-19
Double envelopes failed to alter bloc equilibrium. Their sole effect transferred Shas's seventh seat to Likud, as analyst Amit Segal anticipated on Channel 12. The Arab bloc's nineteenth seat, adjudicated via surplus agreements between the Joint List and Ra'am and shifting hands multiple times Thursday by margins of around a thousand votes, ultimately lands with Ra'am. The Committee subjects records to a final integrity review before publishing results in the official gazette; only then can President Isaac Herzog open consultations with party lists. MP swearing-in and the new chamber's constituent session are slated for **10 November**, per AP.
**Implications**
The final outcome petrifies a tie no recount can shake. Netanyahu's bloc falls eight seats short of a majority and the Zionist opposition thirteen; neither can govern without breaking campaign promises. The seat Likud wrests from Shas leaves block sums untouched whilst reshaping internal composition: it strengthens the Prime Minister's party against partners whilst compounding a crisis for Shas, shedding five seats since 2022 and leaving ultra-orthodox parties at 13 alongside UTJ's seven, down from 18 in the outgoing legislature. Netanyahu's fear campaign concentrated right-wing votes in Likud at allies' expense, leaving the overall block stagnant.
A woman walks past a poster featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a market on the eve of Israel's general elections in Ramla, Israel, 14 October 2026 - REUTERS/ AMIR COHEN
At the opposite end, Arab parties' 19 seats nearly double the outgoing Knesset's ten and surpass the 2020 peak of 15. The demonisation strategy against the Arab vote backfired entirely: it galvanised a mass-abstaining electorate into the legislature's arithmetic kingmaker. Worth noting is wasted votes: ~5% of valid ballots—roughly six seats—went to sub-threshold lists, mostly right-of-centre. That wasted vote explains much of the distance keeping Netanyahu from an absolute majority.
**Outlook and Scenarios**

## The complete count confirms the tie: 53-48-19
Proclamation on 4 November brings no changes bar marginal review corrections. The subsequent calendar is strictly timed: Herzog has seven days to consult lists and task the MP best positioned with government formation, who gets 28 days, extendable by 14. Should they fail, the president can offer a second candidate, then the Knesset a third; failing all, **Israel** heads to fresh elections in spring 2027, with Netanyahu acting as caretaker PM throughout. Precisely that is the PM's trump card: deadlock does not evict him.
Shin Bet Director Ronen Bar attends a Memorial Day ceremony at Mount Herzl military cemetery in Jerusalem - GIL COHEN-MAGEN / Pool via REUTERS

## Introduction
The counting of double-envelope votes concluded on Thursday afternoon, 29 October, settling—pending official proclamation slated for Wednesday, **4 November**—the outcome of Israel's 27 October elections. Figures confirm what tallies have shown since Wednesday evening: the outgoing coalition bloc led by Benjamin Netanyahu secures **53 seats**, the Zionist opposition spearheaded by former Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot gathers **48**, and the two Arab parties total **19**, an all-time record. Neither major camp reaches the **61 seats** required for an absolute majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
The votes of soldiers, police officers, diplomats, prisoners, and hospitalised citizens shifted just a single piece within the governing block: Likud rises to **27 seats** whilst Shas, the Sephardic ultra-orthodox party, drops to **6**, its lowest tally since 1992.
**Israel** has thus delivered a dual and contradictory verdict. It strips Netanyahu of the majority granted in 2022—his bloc sheds eleven seats in four years—yet awards no one a clear mandate to replace them. An alternative exists in numbers, as 67 MPs reject the Prime Minister, but lacks a program, since that negative majority only rounds out with Arab parties that three of the four Zionist opposition leaders pledged not to approach.
With numbers finalised, battle shifted from counting to legitimacy: Likud claims the election was "stolen" by Arab parties, the Central Elections Committee chair asked Shin Bet to probe foreign funding suspicions, and Police find no backing for fraud claims.
All this unfolds as the Gulf ignites once more. Iran's Revolutionary Guard asserts several tankers struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran has yet to reply to US Vice President JD Vance's letter, and **the United States** has asked allies to prepare for a potential resumption of strikes against Iran following the **3 November** midterms.
Forming the next Israeli government, a routine exercise in parliamentary arithmetic during normal times, has turned into a national security equation. This report analyses developments over the past twenty-four hours, their implications, and unfolding scenarios.

## The complete count confirms the tie: 53-48-19
**Facts**
The Central Elections Committee, an independent body chaired by Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, wrapped up counting double-envelope ballots on Thursday afternoon, having kicked off at 01:00 in the Knesset car park in Jerusalem.
According to figures published by _Israel Hayom_, **5,589,836 votes** were tallied across 12,644 polling stations and counting lots—673 corresponding to double envelopes—with 5,564,764 valid and 25,072 invalid. Turnout hit **77.7%**, the highest since 1999, with Arab mobilisation around **80%** compared to roughly 54% in 2022.
Benny Gantz - REUTERS/ NIR ELIAS
The final breakdown stands as follows: Likud, **27 seats**; Yashar!, Eisenkot's party, **21**; B'Yachad, Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid's list, **12**; the Joint List, **11**; Yair Golan's Democrats, **8**; Ra'am, **8**; Avigdor Lieberman's Yisrael Beytenu, **7**; United Judaism of Torah (UTJ), **7**; Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit, **7**; Shas, **6**; and Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism-Zehut, **6**. Likud secures **20.5%** of valid votes and Yashar!, **16.1%**. Yoaz Hendel's Reservists (**2.72%**) and retired general Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael (**1.68%**) fall beneath the 3.25% threshold, equating to roughly 180,900 votes under the full count.

## The complete count confirms the tie: 53-48-19
Double envelopes failed to alter bloc equilibrium. Their sole effect transferred Shas's seventh seat to Likud, as analyst Amit Segal anticipated on Channel 12. The Arab bloc's nineteenth seat, adjudicated via surplus agreements between the Joint List and Ra'am and shifting hands multiple times Thursday by margins of around a thousand votes, ultimately lands with Ra'am. The Committee subjects records to a final integrity review before publishing results in the official gazette; only then can President Isaac Herzog open consultations with party lists. MP swearing-in and the new chamber's constituent session are slated for **10 November**, per AP.
**Implications**
The final outcome petrifies a tie no recount can shake. Netanyahu's bloc falls eight seats short of a majority and the Zionist opposition thirteen; neither can govern without breaking campaign promises. The seat Likud wrests from Shas leaves block sums untouched whilst reshaping internal composition: it strengthens the Prime Minister's party against partners whilst compounding a crisis for Shas, shedding five seats since 2022 and leaving ultra-orthodox parties at 13 alongside UTJ's seven, down from 18 in the outgoing legislature. Netanyahu's fear campaign concentrated right-wing votes in Likud at allies' expense, leaving the overall block stagnant.
A woman walks past a poster featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a market on the eve of Israel's general elections in Ramla, Israel, 14 October 2026 - REUTERS/ AMIR COHEN
At the opposite end, Arab parties' 19 seats nearly double the outgoing Knesset's ten and surpass the 2020 peak of 15. The demonisation strategy against the Arab vote backfired entirely: it galvanised a mass-abstaining electorate into the legislature's arithmetic kingmaker. Worth noting is wasted votes: ~5% of valid ballots—roughly six seats—went to sub-threshold lists, mostly right-of-centre. That wasted vote explains much of the distance keeping Netanyahu from an absolute majority.
**Outlook and Scenarios**

## The complete count confirms the tie: 53-48-19
Proclamation on 4 November brings no changes bar marginal review corrections. The subsequent calendar is strictly timed: Herzog has seven days to consult lists and task the MP best positioned with government formation, who gets 28 days, extendable by 14. Should they fail, the president can offer a second candidate, then the Knesset a third; failing all, **Israel** heads to fresh elections in spring 2027, with Netanyahu acting as caretaker PM throughout. Precisely that is the PM's trump card: deadlock does not evict him.

Likud secures **20.5%** of valid votes and Yashar!, **16.1%**. Yoaz Hendel's Reservists (**2.72%**) and retired general Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael (**1.68%**) fall beneath the 3.25% threshold, equating to roughly 180,900 votes under the full count.

## The complete count confirms the tie: 53-48-19
Double envelopes failed to alter bloc equilibrium. Their sole effect transferred Shas's seventh seat to Likud, as analyst Amit Segal anticipated on Channel 12. The Arab bloc's nineteenth seat, adjudicated via surplus agreements between the Joint List and Ra'am and shifting hands multiple times Thursday by margins of around a thousand votes, ultimately lands with Ra'am. The Committee subjects records to a final integrity review before publishing results in the official gazette; only then can President Isaac Herzog open consultations with party lists. MP swearing-in and the new chamber's constituent session are slated for **10 November**, per AP.
**Implications**
The final outcome petrifies a tie no recount can shake. Netanyahu's bloc falls eight seats short of a majority and the Zionist opposition thirteen; neither can govern without breaking campaign promises. The seat Likud wrests from Shas leaves block sums untouched whilst reshaping internal composition: it strengthens the Prime Minister's party against partners whilst compounding a crisis for Shas, shedding five seats since 2022 and leaving ultra-orthodox parties at 13 alongside UTJ's seven, down from 18 in the outgoing legislature. Netanyahu's fear campaign concentrated right-wing votes in Likud at allies' expense, leaving the overall block stagnant.
A woman walks past a poster featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a market on the eve of Israel's general elections in Ramla, Israel, 14 October 2026 - REUTERS/ AMIR COHEN
At the opposite end, Arab parties' 19 seats nearly double the outgoing Knesset's ten and surpass the 2020 peak of 15. The demonisation strategy against the Arab vote backfired entirely: it galvanised a mass-abstaining electorate into the legislature's arithmetic kingmaker. Worth noting is wasted votes: ~5% of valid ballots—roughly six seats—went to sub-threshold lists, mostly right-of-centre. That wasted vote explains much of the distance keeping Netanyahu from an absolute majority.
**Outlook and Scenarios**

## The complete count confirms the tie: 53-48-19
Proclamation on 4 November brings no changes bar marginal review corrections. The subsequent calendar is strictly timed: Herzog has seven days to consult lists and task the MP best positioned with government formation, who gets 28 days, extendable by 14. Should they fail, the president can offer a second candidate, then the Knesset a third; failing all, **Israel** heads to fresh elections in spring 2027, with Netanyahu acting as caretaker PM throughout. Precisely that is the PM's trump card: deadlock does not evict him.
Shin Bet Director Ronen Bar attends a Memorial Day ceremony at Mount Herzl military cemetery in Jerusalem - GIL COHEN-MAGEN / Pool via REUTERS

The Court held that because a majority wanted to replace the Speaker,
the Speaker must allow for such a vote to reflect election results. MKs’ right
to elect a Speaker warrants special protection during the COVID -19 crisis ,
which involved the exertion of emergency powers that greatly infringed upon
constitutional rights. 38 A further justification was Edelstein’s carryover
position as a stand -in for a caretaker government whose tenure carried
through a third election cycle. 39 The Court cited my work for the proposition
that a caretaker government suffers from a democratic deficit, and this is
especially true after elections, when t he people’s will has already been
expressed. Thus, there is a greater need for parliamentary supervision of the
caretaker government’s actions. 40
People unfamiliar with current Israeli politics might have trouble
comprehending this constitutional crisis’ s magnitude. The Court used a
neutral tone that failed to capture Israel’s state of polarization. The Court
failed to mention that the decision was given at a time in which Prime
Minister (“PM”) Benjamin Netanyahu, who headed the caretaker
government, was Israel’s first indicted sitting PM. It also did not note that
multiple petitioners petitioned the Court several times against an indicted
PM’s continued tenure. 41 Nor did it note that Speaker Edelstein belonged to
Netanyahu’s party.
The Court noted th at Edelstein feared that the new emerging Knesset
majority sought to elect a permanent Speaker to pass “controversial
legislation,” 42 but did not elaborate on this legislation’s nature and why
petitioners were intent on passing it as soon as possible. In fact, this
“controversial legislation” sought to amend Israel’s Basic Laws to prevent a
criminally indicted person from forming and heading a government. 43
Israel is a constitutional democracy. The Knesset enacts and amends
Basic Laws using its regular legislative process. Each Basic Law deals with
a particular state institution or constitutional rights and principles. Despite

### Surplus-vote agreements
Knesset MK Sami Abu Shehadeh announced on 14 January 2021 that he would run for the leadership of Balad.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-15) MK and former leader Mtanes Shehadeh sought re-election. The party held primaries on 23 January 2021 for its leader and its list for Knesset. The Balad council, which consists of a total of 600 members, were eligible to vote in Nazareth.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-16) Abu Shehadeh was elected party leader by the Central Committee, with a total of 230 votes.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-17)
Stav Shaffir was re-elected as the head of Green Party on 29 January 2021.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-jpost30jan-18)

### Surplus-vote agreements
On 5 January, incumbent Jewish Home party leader Rafi Peretz stated that he would not head the party and would not stand for re-election, but did not rule out a return to politics in the future.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-isratimes4jan-19)Nir Orbach announced he would run for the leadership slot.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-20)Hagit Moshe also ran (at Netanyahu's request).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-21) The party's Central Committee selected its chair and party list, rather than holding a vote amongst party members.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-22) Moshe was elected party leader by the Central Committee on 19 January 2021.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-23) Party primaries were held on 26 January.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-24)

### Surplus-vote agreements
The Tel Aviv District Court ruled on 3 January 2021 that primaries for Labor's Knesset list and leadership must take place, despite the fact that Amir Peretz and his supporters voted in favor of canceling them. MK Merav Michaeli announced she would run for party leadership shortly after.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-25) Gil Beilin announced he would run on 11 January.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-26) The Israeli High Court rejected an appeal by the Labor party, ensuring that all party members (instead of just committee members) will be able to vote in the primary.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-27) Former Labor leader Ehud Barak announced on 18 January that he would not run,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-28) while Itzik Shmuli announced the next day that he would not run. Avi Shaked and David Landsman,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-29) Ethiopian immigrant Yitzhak Time,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-30) and Na'ava Katz also ran.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-31)
The vote for party leader was won by Michaeli on 24 January.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-32)

### Surplus-vote agreements
The deadline for entering the Knesset primary was extended to 30 January; 59 candidates entered the race.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-jpost30jan-18) The primary election for choosing the Knesset slate took place 1 February.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-33)
The Likud was ordered by its internal court to have its Constitutional Committee meet by 30 December to begin preparations for the selection of candidates for its electoral slate, following a petition filed by members of the party's Central Committee.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-34) The party's Constitution Committee voted on 30 December to cancel party primaries,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-35) which was made official on 2 January 2021.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-36)
Meretz would have held a leadership election on 13 January 2021, while a primary for the rest of its electoral list would have been held on 21 January.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-37) However, the party decided on 3 January 2021 to not hold primaries as no one challenged Nitzan Horowitz, the party leader.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Israeli_legislative_election#cite_note-38)

Israeli Supreme Court Justice Yitzhak Amit became President (Chief Justice) of the Supreme Court on Sunday, January 26! He was elected by the Judicial Selection Committee, over which Netanyahu's government has only partial influence, rather than the veto control it seeks in order to neutralize the court's independence.
Now Israel's government, through its Justice Minister Yariv Levin, is vowing not to recognize Amit's election (!). This is an unprecedented step, creating a constitutional crisis that threatens Israel's system of checks-and-balances and pushes it further toward hollow democracy and authoritarianism.
